narrative:
FCRA 605B ( 15 U.S.C. 1681c-2 ) ( a ) Block. Except as otherwise provided in this section, a consumer reporting agency shall block the reporting of any information in the file of a consumer that the consumer identifies as information that resulted from an alleged identity theft, not later than 4 business days after the date of receipt by such agency of ( 1 ) appropriate proof of the identity of the consumer ; ( 2 ) a copy of an identity theft report ; ( 3 ) the identification of such information by the consumer; and ( 4 ) a statement by the consumer that the information is not information relating to any transaction by the consumer.

( b ) Notification. A consumer reporting agency shall promptly notify the furnisher of information identified by the consumer under subsection ( a ) of this section ( 1 ) that the information may be a result of identity theft ; ( 2 ) that an identity theft report has been filed ; ( 3 ) that a block has been requested under this section; and ( 4 ) of the effective dates of the block.

( c ) Authority to decline or rescind.

( 1 ) In general. A consumer reporting agency may decline to block, or may rescind any block, of information relating to a consumer under this section, if the consumer reporting agency reasonably determines that ( A ) the information was blocked in error or a block was requested by the consumer in error ; ( B ) the information was blocked, or a block was requested by the consumer, on the basis of a material misrepresentation of fact by the consumer relevant to the request to block ; or ( C ) the consumer obtained possession of goods, services, or money as a result of the blocked transaction or transactions.

( 2 ) Notification to consumer. If a block of information is declined or rescinded under this subsection, the affected consumer shall be notified promptly, in the same manner as consumers are notified of the reinsertion of information under section 1681i ( a ) ( 5 ) ( B ) of this title.

( 3 ) Significance of block. For purposes of this subsection, if a consumer reporting agency rescinds a block, the presence of information in the file of a consumer prior to the blocking of such information is not evidence of whether the consumer knew or should have known that the consumer obtained possession of any goods, services, or money as a result of the block.

( d ) Exception for resellers.

( 1 ) No reseller file. This section shall not apply to a consumer reporting agency, if the consumer reporting agency ( A ) is a reseller ; ( B ) is not, at the time of the request of the consumer under subsection ( a ) of this section, otherwise furnishing or reselling a consumer report concerning the information identified by the consumer ; and ( C ) informs the consumer, by any means, that the consumer may report the identity theft to the Bureau to obtain consumer information regarding identity theft.

( 2 ) Reseller with file. The sole obligation of the consumer reporting agency under this section, with regard to any request of a consumer under this section, shall be to block the consumer report maintained by the consumer reporting agency from any subsequent use, if ( A ) the consumer, in accordance with the provisions of subsection ( a ) of this section, identifies, to a consumer reporting agency, information in the file of the consumer that resulted from identity theft ; and ( B ) the consumer reporting agency is a reseller of the identified information.

( 3 ) Notice. In carrying out its obligation under paragraph ( 2 ), the reseller shall promptly provide a notice to the consumer of the decision to block the file. Such notice shall contain the name, address, and telephone number of each consumer reporting agency from which the consumer information was obtained for resale.

( e ) Exception for verification companies. The provisions of this section do not apply to a check services company, acting as such, which issues authorizations for the purpose of approving or processing negotiable instruments, electronic fund transfers, or similar methods of payments, except that, beginning 4 business days after receipt of information described in paragraphs ( 1 ) through ( 3 ) of subsection ( a ) of this section, a check services company shall not report to a national consumer reporting agency described in section 1681a ( p ) of this title, any information identified in the subject identity theft report as resulting from identity theft.

( f ) Access to blocked information by law enforcement agencies. No provision of this section shall be construed as requiring a consumer reporting agency to prevent a Federal, State, or local law enforcement agency from accessing blocked information in a consumer file to which the agency could otherwise obtain access under this subchapter

narrative:
CFPB Complaint Against Bank of America for Denial of Bill of Exchange Complaint Summary : Bank of America ( BOA ) has denied acceptance of a Bill of Exchange ( Sight Draft ) presented by PRINCIPAL ; XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citing the requirement of having a business account for over three years, an excellent credit score, and a minimum balance. This decision violates federal and state laws governing negotiable instruments, deprives the principal of rightful financial benefits, and demonstrates potential unjust enrichment through unauthorized use of the principals information.

Violations Cited : Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ) Compliance UCC 3-104 : A Bill of Exchange meets the definition of a negotiable instrument. It must be honored if validly presented.

UCC 3-501 & 4-301 : BOA has a duty to process and handle presentment of negotiable instruments appropriately and promptly.

31 CFR 328.5 ( b ) : BOA must process financial instruments intended for book-entry securities conversion when presented according to the regulation.

Consumer Financial Protection Act ( 12 U.S.C. 5531 & 5536 ) : BOA 's restrictive policies may constitute an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice ( UDAAP ), preventing legitimate financial transactions.

Unjust Enrichment Allegation : BOA benefits from the principals information ( e.g., account details, transactional data ) without compensating for its financial use or reporting such benefits to regulatory agencies like the SEC, Federal Reserve, or IRS.

Fiat Currency Context and Federal Law Compliance : All U.S. currency is fiat-based, and BOAs restrictive policies on processing negotiable instruments contradict the fundamental nature of modern banking under U.S. monetary law.

Requested Actions : Immediate Acceptance of the Bill of Exchange ( Sight Draft ) : Process the draft for {$150000.00} USD, ensuring compliance with federal laws, UCC provisions, and BOAs fiduciary responsibilities.

Registration with Federal Reserve : Register the principals active Revocable Trust account with the Federal Reserve for online banking, Fedwire processing, and discount window participation.

Forensic Audit of BOA Practices : Conduct an independent forensic audit to identify instances of unjust enrichment or unauthorized benefits derived from the principals information.

Securities Handling and SEC Reporting : If BOA converts the Bill of Exchange into book-entry securities, ensure compliance with the Securities Act of 1933 and 1934, including registration and disclosure requirements.

Relevant Benefits to BOA for Accepting the Bill of Exchange : Securitization and Liquidity Creation : BOA can securitize the Bill of Exchange, converting it into tradable financial assets.

Securitization benefits BOA by creating liquidity and opening opportunities for investment and revenue generation.

Strengthened Capital Position : The Bill of Exchange enhances BOA 's financial portfolio and strengthens its capital reserves.

Compliance and Customer Trust : Accepting valid negotiable instruments bolsters customer trust and aligns with regulatory compliance.

Resolution Sought : The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is requested to investigate BOA for these practices, ensure corrective actions are taken, and mandate BOAs adherence to relevant laws, including : UCC Articles 3 and 4, 31 CFR 328.5 ( b ), Federal Reserve and SEC regulations, and Federal protections under 12 U.S.C. 5531 and 5536.

By addressing this complaint, BOA will ensure compliance with financial laws, enhance operational benefits, and restore fair treatment for its customers.

You can incorporate the timing details and mention of the replacement card into the existing narrative like this : On Friday, XX/XX/2024, I received notice that my account was closed due to " one or more occurrences of late or returned payments in the last six months. '' However, after speaking with a representative XXXX XXXX, Reference # XXXX ), I was told there were no late payments but three returned payments : on XXXX and XXXX for {$600.00} each, and on XXXX for {$6900.00}. 

The returned payments were caused by a misleading " Apply '' button located next to the " Other Amount '' input field on the payment page. The button, now removed, led to confusion about its purpose, causing the unintended submission of payments. When I realized the error, I was told the initial payments could not be canceled, putting me in a dire financial position. This also triggered the additional returned payments. The screenshots attached show the " Apply '' button before its removal and the updated interface. 

When the returned payments occurred, I contacted customer service and was assured they would be forgiven, with no penalties applied. Relying on this assurance, I continued to use the card and increased my balance, assuming the card would remain available through the holiday season. Now, nearly four months after the returned payments, I find myself facing an unforeseen account closure just days after receiving and activating a replacement card that I can no longer use due to this abrupt action.

This " Apply '' button appears to have been intentionally designed to confuse users, leading to accidental payments. Its placement near the input field, lack of clear communication, and absence of confirmation steps encouraged accidental clicks. Once payments were submitted, they couldnt be canceled, trapping users financially. The companys representatives provided misleading assurances about the impact of the returned payments, further exacerbating harm. 

This deceptive design likely benefited the company through fees from returned payments, late charges, and increased interest on balances. It also justified account closures, allowing the company to recover debt and void user rewards. Changes to the website obscured the misleading design and hindered dispute resolution. These actions suggest a deliberate strategy to exploit users for financial gain. I urge the CFPB to investigate this practice, provide restitution, and ensure similar actions are prevented in the future. 

In addition, when I was transferred to an Adverse Action Department representative ( XXXX ) regarding the closure of my account, I was told that the Adverse Action Department does not record or provide reference numbers for call occurrences. This practice, if true, appears to benefit the company by limiting accountability, as customers can not easily prove what was said during a call or verify assurances provided by representatives. It also hinders dispute resolution, making it more challenging for customers to follow up or contest adverse decisions without a record of the interaction. Furthermore, the lack of reference numbers reduces the companys exposure to legal or regulatory scrutiny, as there is less documented evidence available for review in case of complaints or investigations. This opacity also obscures the companys internal practices, making it difficult to confirm whether policies are being followed consistently. Additionally, the absence of reference numbers may discourage customers from pursuing complaints, as it creates frustration and a perception that their concerns will not be addressed effectively. By minimizing the documentation of such interactions, the company reduces its likelihood of having to offer restitution or reverse adverse decisions, further benefiting from this lack of transparency.

sub_issue: Funds not handled or disbursed as instructed
narrative:
I previously submitted a complaint on my own behalf, asking Wells Fargo to provide me the {$520.00} bonus I was promised for opening a savings account, depositing {$25000.00} into it within 30 days of account opening, and keeping it there for the required time ( 90 days after account opening ). Wells Fargo responded that because I transferred {$17.00} in rewards cash from my Wells Fargo credit card to meet the {$25000.00} deposit requirement, I did not fulfil the requirement to deposit {$25000.00} in " new money '' to the savings account in order to qualify for the {$520.00} bonus. 

While I understand that Wells Fargo has decided not to grant me the {$520.00} bonus I was promised, I file this new complaint to ask that Wells Fargo change its practices by letting customers know when they have not fulfilled the requirements for a bonus, rather than simply allowing the customer to believe they have fulfilled the requirements and look forward to receiving the bonus for months, only to be told upon the customer 's inquiry months later that they will not be receiving the bonus after all, in my case due to a technicality relating to 0.08 % of the deposit requirement. 

What I find most reprehensible is that in cases like mine, which Im sure is not unique, Wells Fargo : 1 ) is aware that the customer has opened the account with the expectation of the {$520.00} bonus, as the customer makes an appointment with a banker and provides him/her a code to receive the bonus ; 2 ) is aware that the customer has not fulfilled the requirements of the bonus at day 30 ; 3 ) does not inform the customer that he/she has not fulfilled the requirements ; 4 ) allows the customer to leave the {$25000.00} in his/her savings account earning very little interest for an additional 90 days ( requirement is for the customer to leave the money in the account until 90 days after account opening, but Wells Fargo has another 30 days to deposit the bonus into the customers account ) ; and 5 ) even at that point, Wells Fargo does not inform the customer that the bonus they were expecting is not forthcoming. 

In sum, Wells Fargo knows the customer is opening the account for the purpose of receiving the bonus, knows after Day 30 that the customer has not fulfilled the requirements for the bonus, does not inform the customer of this, and then to the customers great disappointment only informs them the bonus is not forthcoming over 90 days later when the customer inquires as to what happened to their bonus. All the while, Wells Fargo benefits from withholding the information about the customer not qualifying for the bonus, as the customers {$25000.00} accrues very little interest. I understand that Wells Fargo accrues greater profits by not informing the customer they havent met the bonus requirements, but I consider withholding this information to be a deceptive practice that should stop, and I implore Wells Fargo to change its practices and affirmatively inform its customers that they did not meet the bonus requirements rather than to profit off of customers misunderstandings of the bonus terms.

Dear CFPB, I am writing to file a formal complaint against Navy Federal Credit Union for the unlawful closure of my credit card account, which took place on XX/XX/year>. The circumstances surrounding the closure of this account raise serious concerns regarding potential violations of several federal consumer protection laws, and I am seeking the CFPB 's immediate intervention in this matter. 

Background of the Situation : On XX/XX/year>, I was contacted by a representative from Navy Federal 's in-house collections team regarding my credit card account, which was two months past due. During this conversation, I was informed of financial hardship options designed to keep my account active. The representative assured me that my interest rate would be reduced to 3 % for a period of 12 months and that Navy Federal would be evaluating my eligibility for an additional financial program. At no point was I informed that my account was under consideration for closure. 

However, on XX/XX/year>, just three days later and prior to receiving any further communication about my eligibility for the financial program, Navy Federal closed my account without notice. This abrupt action was unexpected and contrary to the information provided during the XX/XX/XXXX call, during which I was led to believe that my account was still active and being reviewed for assistance. 

Violations of Consumer Protection Laws : Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) Violation : Navy Federals failure to provide complete and accurate information about the status of my account during our XX/XX/XXXX conversation violates the FCRA. The closure of the account without proper notification has likely caused adverse effects on my credit report, and I was not given an opportunity to address or prevent this negative outcome. 
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ) Violation : The communication from Navy Federal was misleading, as I was led to believe that my account was being offered hardship options and would remain active. The sudden closure of the account, without disclosing that it was being targeted for shutdown, constitutes deceptive and unfair collection practices, in violation of the FDCPA. 

Breach of Good Faith and Fair Dealing : By failing to inform me of the true status of my account and then closing it without warning, Navy Federal breached the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. I was denied the opportunity to make informed decisions regarding my account and was misled into believing that it was being maintained in good standing. 

Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) Violation : Navy Federals actions may also constitute a violation of TILA, which requires creditors to provide clear and accurate disclosures about the terms and conditions of credit. The failure to inform me of the impending closure of my account while discussing potential hardship programs falls short of these requirements.
